title: The Ferrari 365 GTC/4 Is Far More than a Discount Daytona

body_markdown:
Let us be brutally honest: The classic car world can be fundamentally shallow. It is a place where a single styling quirk or lack of cinematic provenance can banish a genuinely brilliant motorcar to the shadows. For more than 50 years, the Ferrari 365 GTC/4 has been the victim of this superficiality. It is the perennial bridesmaid, the *other* 1970s V-12, dismissed by purists who affectionately refer to it as *Il Gobbone* , the hunchback. Its crime? It dared to follow the 365 GTB/4 Daytona. And, perhaps more fatally, it dared to wear a rubber nose.


Broad Arrow


But the accepted narrative that the GTC/4 is the ugly, softer sibling is utter nonsense. Specified in the right hue, ideally Blu Sera (metallic blue), Pino Verde (metallic dark green), or a brooding Grigio (gray) that camouflages that contentious matte-black front bumper, the GTC/4 reveals itself as a masterpiece of 1970s wedge design. Stripped of the aesthetic clash, it possesses a more cohesive profile than the[Daytona](https://www.hagerty.com/media/entertainment/the-miami-vice-california-daytona-spyder-the-tv-car-enzo-ferrari-despised/) . More importantly, if you actually want to drive your classic Ferrari rather than brag about it, the GTC/4 is comfortably superior.


Rewind to the 1971 Geneva Motor Show. Ferrari had a problem. The Daytona was a spectacular piece of theatrical violence, a 170-mph hammer for the autostrada. But Ferrari’s core clientele, the wealthy industrialists who kept the lights on in Maranello, wanted something more civilized. They wanted a replacement for the 365 GTC and 365 GT 2+2 lineage, a genuine Grand Tourer with long legs, acceptable luggage space, and everyday civility.


The task fell to Pininfarina, with the shape credited to Filippo Sapino. He brought Maranello kicking and screaming into the 1970s, swapping the voluptuous curves of the previous decade for sharp creases, a fastback silhouette, and an incredibly low hood line. Bodies were fabricated by Pininfarina in Turin, using steel, save for an aluminum hood and trunk lid, before being shipped to Modena for final assembly.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


The most contentious element was that front bumper. An early concession to changing impact expectations—especially in the U.S., where the 5-mph impact bumper mandate was due to take effect for 1973—Sapino integrated it as a wraparound ring housing the grille, sidelights, and indicators. Contrasted against resale red, it can look faintly ridiculous. Paint the car in a dark hue, though, and the bumper recedes, leaving a shark-nosed profile punctuated by pop-up headlamps and neatly blistered arches housing five-spoke Cromodora alloy wheels and suitably chunky Michelin rubber.


To achieve that aggressively low prow, Ferrari’s engineers engaged in some gloriously Italian mechanical gymnastics. Underneath, the C/4 uses a tubular steel chassis closely related to the Daytona’s, with the wheelbase stretched by 100 mm (about 4 inches) to accommodate two hilariously cramped rear seats that effectively serve as a heavily upholstered parcel shelf.


But the Daytona’s towering downdraft carburetors would not fit beneath Sapino’s rakish hood. Consequently, Ferrari binned that arrangement and fitted six twin-choke side-draft Weber 38 DCOE carbs. This pragmatic workaround accidentally created the C/4’s greatest party trick: With the intakes breathing against the bulkhead, the induction howl is piped straight into the cabin. A Daytona sounds magnificent from the pavement, but from the driver’s seat, the GTC/4 has a strong claim to being the best-sounding front-engined Ferrari road car of its era.


Broad Arrow


Mechanically, the C/4 was a radical departure aimed squarely at grand touring usability. Where the Daytona used dry-sump lubrication and a rear-mounted transaxle, the C/4 adopted a wet-sump system with a five-speed manual gearbox mounted conventionally behind the engine. Despite abandoning the transaxle layout, Maranello still achieved an excellent weight distribution by pushing the V-12 deep into the chassis. Output was eased back from the Daytona’s 352 horsepower to 340 hp in European specification, or around 316 hp for federalized U.S. cars.


On the road, the C/4 makes its ultimate case. The Daytona is famously a physical ordeal. It has unassisted steering that requires Popeye forearms at parking speeds, a heavy clutch, a dog-leg gearbox, and a ride that can feel punishing on poor roads. You exit a Daytona after three hours feeling like you have been in a pub brawl.


The C/4, by contrast, is a revelation. Ferrari fitted beautifully weighted ZF hydraulic power steering that retains feedback without the wrestling match. It features a conventional H-pattern gearbox, alongside a self-levelling hydropneumatic rear suspension system. It also came with electric windows and standard air conditioning, which matters enormously if your fantasy of 1970s Ferrari ownership involves more than polishing it under strip lights.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


The driver-focused cockpit could be trimmed with the model’s distinctive tartan cloth inserts, known as Panno, which look magnificent in the correct period context and grip you properly through corners. Full leather was available, but the cloth suits the car’s faintly louche character better. It says you are there to drive, not merely to pose.


Period road tests had the GTC/4 reaching 60 mph in around seven seconds, with 160 mph within reach. More importantly, it does that without making you sweat. *MotorTrend* called it the most refined, flexible and comfortable car Maranello had built to date, and *Road & Track* praised its lighter controls, reduced mechanical thrash, and delicious ease of use. They were bang on the money.


So why the massive disparity in the classifieds? Why is a car that is rarer, better sounding, and infinitely nicer to drive worth a fraction of its sibling?


Broad Arrow


The reality of ownership provides the grim, wallet-emptying answer. Remember those glorious side-draft Webers? They sit exactly where your mechanic does not want them. When the time comes to adjust the valve clearances, and on a Colombo V-12 that time is never as far away as you would like, the carburetors, linkages, and associated plumbing have to come off. Furthermore, the twin Marelli distributors are buried at the back of the camshafts, hard against the firewall. It is a labor-intensive nightmare involving hours of swearing, skinned knuckles, and back-breaking contortion. The Daytona, with its central downdraft arrangement, is easier by comparison. Throw in the cost of expensive Michelin XWX rubber and maintaining that Koni self-levelling rear suspension, and bills mount rapidly.


This terrifying maintenance reputation spooked buyers in the 1980s and ’90s, suppressing values and leading some C/4s into the hands of owners who could not afford to run them properly. But today, the market has matured. We have collectively accepted that keeping a 1970s V-12 Ferrari roadworthy requires deep pockets regardless of the model. The running costs are a known quantity.


Looking at the financials, the C/4 starts to resemble one of the more interesting buys in the classic Ferrari world. Ferrari built 1284 Daytona coupes. By comparison, only 505 copies of the 365 GTC/4 were made during its brief two-year production run. It is properly, wonderfully rare.


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Broad Arrow


Yet[a good, usable Daytona](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/365_gtb!!4/1971/1971-ferrari-365_gtb!!4-daytona?id=aCn1I000000DHPmSAO) will typically relieve you of roughly $480K–$540K, with stronger cars and exceptional examples now topping out around $800K. The Ferrari 365 GTC/4?[A solid, #3 (good) driver](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/365_gtc!!4/1971/1971-ferrari-365_gtc!!4-base?id=aCn1I000000DTb5SAG) is more commonly $165K–$215K territory, with excellent #2 cars more like $235K–$280K and the very best, rarest, or most interesting examples around $300K. Hagerty has tracked[eight auction sales](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/past-sales/1971-ferrari-365_gtc!!4?maxPrice=265000&minPrice=106400&timePeriod=1Y) in the last 12 months, both online and in person, with an average price of $191K.[One of those GT/4s](https://www.broadarrowauctions.com/vehicles/ql26_r0022/1971-ferrari-365-gtc-4-ex-sergio-pininfarina) , Sergio Pininfarina’s very own car—mechanically restored 10 years ago and cosmetically sorted five years ago—brought a “scant” $240K at Broad Arrow’s Quail Auction in August. It’s worth noting that the three highest sales recorded in our database (topped by a $561,000 result for s/n 15933, a ’72 model at Gooding Christie’s Pebble Beach Auction) all came at the height of the classic Ferrari market, in 2015. That very same s/n 15933 (pictured here)[sold again](https://www.broadarrowauctions.com/vehicles/am23_017/1972-ferrari-365-gtc-4) at Broad Arrow’s Amelia Island Auction for $329,500.


For roughly a third of the price of a Daytona, then, you get a much rarer car, a vastly superior driving experience, the greatest induction noise this side of a 1960s Formula 1 grid, and a wedge-shaped profile that has aged gracefully, if not spectacularly. It is the thinking enthusiast’s classic V-12 Ferrari.


Just buy a dark blue one, and never mention the words rubber nose.
